beats.intro: Lesson twenty-seven. [[sub]]The two hardest reviews, the blast and the ace, and the practical questions around every review.
beats.blast: Sometimes you face a major performance problem: someone who, unless things turn around, could lose their job. The review becomes a blast. [[stairs]]Grove shows the stages people climb in resolving a conflict like this. [[ign]]At first, a poor performer tends to ignore the problem. You need facts and examples to show it is real. [[deny]]Then they actively deny it. Odd as it sounds, that is progress. [[blame]]More evidence, and they admit there is a problem, but not theirs. They blame others, a standard defense.
beats.step: Things tend to get stuck here. [[resp]]The biggest step is to assume responsibility: it is my problem. [[work]]That is fateful, because it means work. If it is mine, I have to do something, and it will be unpleasant. [[sol]]Once they take that step, finding the solution is fairly easy. [[emo]]Moving from blame to responsibility is an emotional step. Moving to a solution is an intellectual one, and easier. [[job]]Your job is to get them to responsibility. The solution you find together. [[track]]Keep track of the stage. Jump to solutions while they still deny or blame, and nothing happens.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which stage is it?
beats.outcomes: A blast can end three ways. [[one]]One: they accept your assessment and your cure. [[two]]Two: they disagree with the assessment, but commit to the cure. [[three]]Three: they disagree and won't commit. [[ok]]Which are acceptable? Grove says any outcome that includes a commitment to action. [[agree]]Complex issues rarely win full agreement. Try for it, up to a point. [[comfort]]But don't confuse emotional comfort with operational need. You need their commitment, not their agreement.
beats.convince: Grove learned this in one of his first reviews. [[push]]He kept trying to persuade his report to see it his way. [[andy]]Finally the man said: Andy, you'll never convince me. But why do you need to? I've already said I will do what you say. [[shut]]Grove stopped, embarrassed. Much later he saw why. His insistence was about making himself feel better, not about running the business.
beats.power: What if you can't get past blame? [[role]]Then step into the formal role of the boss. You may be right, or I may be. But the organization requires me to give you instructions, and this is what I want you to do. [[mon]]Get their commitment, then monitor against it. [[story]]Grove once found a review written by one of his managers superficial. The manager agreed, but would not spend time rewriting it. [[insist]]Grove said: I want you to do it. The integrity of the review system matters more to me than to you. [[okay]]Okay, said the manager, and rewrote it well. His own report got the better review, and never knew about the disagreement.
beats.ace: Now the ace. [[twenty]]Grove had about twenty middle managers analyze reviews they had received. [[high]]They were achievers. Their reviews were high and well written. [[retro]]But they looked back. Most said little about how to improve, or even how to stay at that level. [[poor]]Poor performers, meanwhile, get detailed corrective action programs. [[rev]]Grove says we have it reversed. [[lev]]Stars do a disproportionate share of the work, so improving them is high leverage. [[room]]However stellar someone is, there is room to improve. Use hindsight to show even an ace how to do better.
beats.self: Should people write a self-review first? [[cheat]]Imagine your boss takes yours, reformats it, rates it superior, and hands it back. You would feel cheated. [[attn]]And if you must tell your boss what you did, he hasn't been paying attention. [[lead]]A review is a formal act of leadership. Prompted judgment looks false. Commit to your own judgment, up front. [[up]]What about asking your report to review you? That might be a good idea, but it is advisory. [[equal]]You are their leader, and you should never pretend you are equals in a review.
beats.timing: When should they get the written review? Grove tried it three ways. [[after]]After the talk, they may find a phrase they didn't hear and blow up. [[during]]During the talk, they want to read ahead, not discuss paragraph three. [[aloud]]Reading it aloud has the same problem. And they have no time to think, so they walk away muttering, I should have said this. [[before]]Best: give it to them before you meet. They read it alone, react or overreact, and look at the messages again. [[ready]]By the time you sit down, they are ready, both emotionally and rationally.
beats.hundred: The best way to learn reviews is to think hard about the ones you received. [[trad]]If you are lucky, a good tradition is handed down from boss to report. [[prod]]Even so, people need prodding. [[read]]Each year Grove read about a hundred reviews, all of his own reports' and a random sample from across Intel. [[back]]He commented, and sent them back for rewrites or with a compliment, as visibly as he could. [[why]]Because the review is the most important task-relevant feedback we give.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]In a blast, move them up the stairs to responsibility. [[w2]]Commitment to act is enough; agreement is a bonus. [[w3]]If stuck, use your authority, then monitor. [[w4]]Coach your aces too: stars are high leverage. [[w5]]Judge on your own; send the written review first. Now the lesson practice.
